analysis.one_liner: Bans manipulative and deceptive schemes in wholesale electricity markets to protect ratepayers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 9 cosponsors in January 2004, the bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the collapse of Enron, whose traders used deceptive schemes to run up electricity prices, Senator Maria Cantwell proposed writing an explicit ban on market manipulation into the Federal Power Act. The bill would make it unlawful to use any manipulative or deceptive device in the buying or selling of wholesale electricity or transmission service, and would let federal regulators treat prices produced by such schemes as unreasonable. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Electric ratepayers — households and businesses that buy power at wholesale prices. The bill would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission a clear statutory mandate to police manipulation and would let prices inflated by deceptive trading be challenged as unjust and unreasonable [S2][S3]. It would also help honest market participants by discouraging competitors from gaming the market.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a section to the Federal Power Act making it unlawful to use any manipulative or deceptive device in the purchase or sale of electric energy or transmission services under federal jurisdiction [S2][S3].

Amends the just-and-reasonable standard so that rates that result from a manipulative or deceptive device are not considered just and reasonable, creating a basis to challenge manipulated prices [S3].
States the purpose plainly as the protection of electric ratepayers, giving the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rulemaking authority in the public interest for that purpose [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, merchant generators, and others who profit from manipulative or deceptive trading in wholesale power markets. They would face liability under the new prohibition, and enforcement activity would raise compliance and litigation costs for the sector generally.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition only applies to devices used 'in contravention of such regulations as the Commission may promulgate' — so enforcement depends entirely on the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission first writing rules defining what counts as manipulation [S3].
The bill covers only wholesale electricity and transmission sales under federal jurisdiction; it does not reach retail prices or markets outside federal jurisdiction, limiting who it protects [S2].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that a statutory ban adds little unless regulators actively pursue cases, and the bill leaves the pace and vigor of enforcement to the commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and straightforward: it copies a proven approach from securities law (banning deceptive devices in trading) and applies it to electricity markets, where manipulation directly raises prices paid by consumers. Its main weakness is that it delegates the real work to FERC rulemaking, so its value depends on the regulator using the authority. The costs fall on firms that would otherwise manipulate prices, which is the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on January 21, 2004, and no further action was ever recorded before that Congress ended in early January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill for herself, Senator Russ Feingold, and Senator Jim Jeffords on January 21, 2004 [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral [S5].
Nine senators cosponsored the bill — eight Democrats and one Independent — and no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity traders and power marketers benefited, since no statutory manipulation ban was enacted and the federal regulator's authority over manipulative trading remained as unsettled as before. Ratepayers, who the bill named as the party to be protected, gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors [S3].

for.role: Independent senator from Vermont; original cosponsor

against.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the remainder of the 108th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.industry: Wholesale energy traders and power marketers
industries.note: The bill would expose firms that use manipulative or deceptive trading devices to federal liability, and would let prices inflated by such schemes be struck down as unjust and unreasonable [S2][S3]. Traders who profit by gaming power markets lose; honest market participants gain a more level field.

Law-abiding utilities would bear compliance and enforcement exposure but also benefit from clearer rules and more orderly markets, since manipulation by competitors distorts the prices utilities pay and charge [S3].
